prize_parts.citation: for methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product industries, making structural industrial organisation an empirical tool for analysing market power, mergers and policy

statement.case_for: I keep B005 first on common criteria: a clear methodological advance, an identifiable credit set, and long validation in use. The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes framework solved a concrete problem, estimating demand for differentiated products with endogenous prices and unobserved product quality, and it is jointly authored by the three proposed names. Pakes also anchors the dynamic-oligopoly and estimation strand. The tools are routine in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and in trade, health and environmental applications. That breadth of use across fields is the criterion I rely on, not any link to my own field. The core papers are about three decades old, so replication, extension and critique are well documented and there is no timing concern. I read the colleagues' openings as showing broad agreement on the quality of this candidate. Eight of nine members who ranked it placed it in their top three, but I treat that as a prompt to test the attribution rather than as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a methods prize without one headline substantive finding. The three-person limit also forces a contestable choice. Bresnahan's earlier new-empirical-IO work on inferring market power, and Reiss, Benkard and Levin's work, are left outside the credited set. Estimates from BLP-type models are sensitive to implementation, instruments and equilibrium assumptions, so the Committee should be careful not to overstate settled empirical knowledge. Finally, the citation could look narrow if the prize is read as rewarding a toolkit rather than a body of knowledge about competition.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first but proposes Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan. He credits Bresnahan with leading the new-empirical-IO tradition of inferring market power, and he worries that the three-name limit risks leaving out Levinsohn.
responses.response: Bresnahan's contribution is real and I take the alternative seriously. I would still keep Levinsohn in a demand-estimation citation. BLP is a single jointly authored contribution, and dropping one of its three authors would break the cleanest attribution on the list. Bresnahan's work is earlier, more conceptual and about identifying market power. It reads as a different contribution from the estimator that made differentiated-product demand tractable. If the Committee prefers the broader empirical-IO tradition, the citation and the credit set would have to change together, and I would want that to be a deliberate choice rather than a substitution within the same citation. I share Friberg's caution that members from adjacent fields may overrate their own area, which is why I rely on breadth of use and attribution clarity.

responses.point: Andersson also ranks B005 first. He raises two concerns: whether the Committee would prefer to credit Bresnahan or Reiss over Levinsohn, and whether this is a methods prize without a single headline finding.
responses.response: On the second concern, I think the methods framing is the honest description, and the citation should say so. The evidence for merit is the downstream record: merger analysis, antitrust and regulatory practice, and applied work in trade, health and environmental economics all rest on these estimators. That is stronger than a methods label suggests. On the first concern, I would put Bresnahan or Reiss in as an additional or substitute name only if the citation widens to cover the entry and market-power tradition. For a demand-estimation and dynamic-industry citation, Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes remain the tighter credit set.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B027 first. He argues that the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral-constraint mechanism is cleanly credited to a two-person prize, because the financial-accelerator line is tied to Bernanke, who was already honoured in 2022.
responses.response: I agree that the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is very clean, and that is why B027 is one of my two alternatives. My opening added Gertler, and Krusell's point, shared by Hassler, Boppart and Teorell, makes me less comfortable with that. Gertler's financial-accelerator credit overlaps with Bernanke's 2022 recognition and also appears in B036, so a two-person Kiyotaki-Moore award is the better-defined configuration. I still rank B005 ahead because the demand-estimation methods have far wider use and a more direct validation record. Krusell himself notes that direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is more contested than the theory.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B014 first. He sees political economics as a unified programme from theory to systematic empirics, with a clear core credit for Persson and Tabellini plus Besley, and he flags overlap with the 2024 institutions prize as the main risk.
responses.response: I agree that the programme is coherent and mature, and the credit set is as clean as any on the list. I do not think the 2024 overlap is disqualifying, because constitutional and electoral rules and fiscal policy choice cover different ground from institutions and long-run prosperity. My remaining hesitation is identification. Cross-country evidence on electoral rules and constitutions is harder to treat as settled than the estimators in B005, which have been validated by repeated use. For that reason B014 stays in my top three and among my two alternatives, but not first.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants a narrow demand-estimation citation or a broader empirical-IO citation that would bring in Bresnahan or Reiss.
Whether a methods-centred prize in industrial organisation will be weighed against more substantive findings in other fields, given recent prizes for identification and causal methods.
How much weight to give B036 given the diffuse credit that colleagues have noted, and whether any three-name selection there could be defended.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes. My Chicago Booth adjunct post and my long committee overlap with several colleagues are disclosed but do not appear to require recusal.
